clue.text: Native of the north, say, in recession: do _______ ?

indicators.note: receding means going backwards, so the abbreviation for 'say' is read from right to left

parts.note: EG, for example, is what 'say' abbreviates
the blank completes the stock phrase 'do or die', so it supplies the words or die

explanation.surface: A puzzled solver is asked to fill in a blank about a northerner during an economic slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in recession' is the reversal signal, not economics. The blank after 'do' asks for the rest of a well-known motto. A Geordie comes from Tyneside, around Newcastle, in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A Geordie is a person from Newcastle upon Tyne, a city in the north of England.

clue.text: Close to cracking nuts exhibiting an unpleasant texture

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

parts.note: nuts and loopy both mean crazy

explanation.surface: Something near to breaking open nuts has a nasty feel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloopy describes something thick and sticky, an off-putting consistency.

clue.text: 14 (1968), traditional fare, but bacon only?

parts.note: liver and bacon served with nothing but bacon has zero liver, so O, nil
liver, as in the classic British dish liver and bacon

explanation.surface: A film is likened to a classic dish of liver and bacon with only the bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: Liver and bacon is a traditional British dish; with only bacon there is 'O liver'. The film is the musical of Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Carol Reed's musical Oliver! won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 1968.

clue.text: See 28
One presents them briefly with regular parts of scheme

parts.note: them is shortened in speech to 'em

indicators.note: every other letter of the word scheme is taken

explanation.surface: A host gives the shortened ones a regular share of the plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of sCHEME give CEE.
explanation.definitionFit: An emcee is a master of ceremonies, a host who introduces acts.

clue.text: Vicar, you might say, has put 28 in shade

indicators.note: putting one thing in another means the abbreviation is inserted into the description
this word is a container marker: it says one piece is placed inside the other, and the clue words of the pieces show which way round

parts.note: a vicar might be described as a pious gentleman, PI GENT in crossword shorthand
28 across is the sum of a thousand thousand, abbreviated M

explanation.surface: A clergyman has stashed a fortune somewhere out of the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: PI is the usual crossword shortening of pious, so a vicar is a 'pi gent'; 'has put ... in' places the 28 across abbreviation inside that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigment is a colouring substance, and shade can mean a colour or tint.

clue.text: Sound leader's rule

indicators.note: sound signals that the word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a principal is a head or leader, as of a school

explanation.surface: A reliable head teacher's regulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning reliable, but it signals a homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: A principle is a fundamental rule or law of conduct.

clue.text: One's undercarriage providing 14 (1958)

indicators.note: read as 'under carriage': in this down entry the numeral sits under a light two-wheeled carriage, a gig

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A plane's landing gear somehow provides a 1958 film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undercarriage' splits into 'under carriage': in a down entry I goes under GIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigi, the Lerner and Loewe musical, won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 1958.

clue.text: Alter ego that is Paul, not Braveheart: end of story

indicators.note: to alter is to change, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: IE abbreviates id est, that is

indicators.note: not means a letter is removed from the setter's name

parts.note: the heart of the word brave is its middle letter A

explanation.surface: The setter Paul has a second self who is not the hero of Braveheart, closing the tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alter ego' looks like a phrase but 'Alter' is the anagram signal; Paul, the setter, loses A to give PUL.
explanation.definitionFit: An epilogue is the closing section that ends a story or play.

clue.text: Little bit upset about start of movie, one's 14 (1963)

indicators.note: the reversed word goes round the initial letter
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so read from the bottom

parts.note: a jot is a tiny amount

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: one's taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A small thing is upset about the start of a film that is one of the theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' in a down clue turns the word for a little bit upside down; 'about' wraps it round the first letter of movie, and 'one's' is simply the word ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Richardson's Tom Jones won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 1963.

clue.text: College spirit initially turning to love

indicators.note: the first letter of the spirit's name changes into the letter for love

parts.note: Ariel is the airy spirit in Shakespeare's The Tempest
love is nil in tennis scoring, written as O

explanation.surface: University spirit at first is giving way to romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Oriel is a college of Oxford University.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriel is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford.

clue.text: Cold fish my theme, which is transparent

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
ling is a sea fish of the cod family
the setter's theme in this puzzle is Oscar-winning movies, so a film

explanation.surface: A setter describes a chilly fish as the subject of the puzzle, adding that it is see-through.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle's theme is Best Picture winners, so 'my theme' is FILM.
explanation.definitionFit: Cling film is thin clear plastic wrap, a material that can be seen through.

clue.text: Currency sees racketeer Rod back in the money

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the coins named in the clue

parts.note: pence are British coins, money in general

indicators.note: back means the tennis player's surname is read in reverse

parts.note: Rod Laver is a great Australian tennis player, so a wielder of a racket

explanation.surface: A gangster called Rod is back in the cash, making a currency story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racketeer' is a pun: not a gangster but a tennis player with a racket, Rod Laver; 'back' reverses his surname before 'in' puts it inside the coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Currency can mean the state of being widespread or current, which is a sense of prevalence.

clue.text: Sweet game

definitions.meaning: a British brand of ring-shaped mint sweet
a sport played on horseback with mallets

explanation.definitionFit: Polo is both a mint sweet sold in Britain and a team sport played on horseback.

clue.text: Bird finds small dog in basket

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the fishing basket

parts.note: a creel is an angler's wicker basket
a chow is a Chinese breed of dog

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a little dog curled up in a basket.
explanation.definitionFit: The screech owl is a small owl of the Americas, a kind of bird.

clue.text: Feel confident about Braveheart finally, old Scotsman the victor as such

indicators.note: one phrase goes round the other pieces like a ring

parts.note: to feel confident is to be sure

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the film title

parts.note: the Picts were an ancient people of Scotland

explanation.surface: A fan backs the film Braveheart, whose ancient Scottish hero wins the day.
explanation.walkthrough: Braveheart (1995) won the Oscar for Best Picture, so it is 'the victor as such'; the answer is also the theme referred to as 14 elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The winner of the top Academy Award is the film named the year's top movie.

clue.text: About to tuck into short and stout home baking product

indicators.note: tucking into means being placed inside the word for short and stout

parts.note: squat means short and thickset
re means about or concerning
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone short and stout is about to tuck into some home baking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tuck into' suggests eating, but here RE is tucked into SQUAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A square tin is a cake tin with four straight sides, an item for baking.

clue.text: Invention coming together again after disagreement

definitions.meaning: fabrication, as in concocting a story

explanation.definitionFit: Making up means both inventing something and becoming reconciled after a fight.

clue.text: Attila must, given no way out, produce final demands

indicators.note: to produce is to make, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement once the way is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: Attila the Hun, denied an escape route, has to issue ultimatums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given no way out' removes ST from the letters of ATTILA MUST before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimata, plural of ultimatum, are last demands backed by a threat.

parts.note: read as letters, these words are A, then two Ls placed about EVE

explanation.surface: A British school exam is offered as the clue to a 1950 Oscar winner.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an instruction: A, then L and L placed all around EVE, gives A LEVEL. An A level is the English school-leaving exam.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bette Davis film won the Academy Award for top picture in 1950.

clue.text: 14 (1982), the ninth supporting its predecessors

indicators.note: in a down entry, supporting means sitting underneath the other letters

parts.note: the letters before the ninth, I, are G and H
I is the ninth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A ninth item props up those that came before it.
explanation.walkthrough: G AND H are the seventh and eighth letters; I goes below them.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Attenborough's biopic Gandhi won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 1982.

clue.text: It is impulsive putting currency in the news

indicators.note: the currency sits inside the two letters

parts.note: news read as new plus new gives N and N
the euro is the currency of much of Europe

explanation.surface: Something rash puts the euro in the headlines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'impulsive' is a pun: a neuron carries nerve impulses.
explanation.definitionFit: A neuron is a nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses.

clue.text: Bird is following another half way back

indicators.note: following means the short word comes after the other piece
back means the trimmed word is read from right to left
going only half way keeps the first half of the word and drops the rest

parts.note: another bird, so the clue's own word bird is used again

explanation.surface: One bird trails another, flying halfway back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' at the start wants to be the only bird, but 'another' refers to the same word again: 'half way' trims it and 'back' turns it round before 'is' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-legged wading bird with a down-curved bill.

clue.text: Bow tie about to become black, which becomes white, so rarely spotted?

definitions.text: which becomes white, so rarely spotted?

parts.note: a bow is an arc or curve

indicators.note: the word for tie goes round the scorching verb

parts.note: to char is to scorch until black

explanation.surface: A bow tie darkens to black, then turns white, and so is seldom seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the word for tie round the verb for blackening. 'spotted' plays on being seen and on having marks: the hare's coat turns white in winter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic hare grows a white winter coat that blends with snow, making it hard to see.

clue.text: Endless beat about right — to describe this?

indicators.note: the trimmed word goes round the abbreviation
endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: to thump is to beat

explanation.surface: A drum beat is called on to describe itself.
explanation.walkthrough: THUMP loses its last letter to make THUM, which goes round R.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrum is a steady rhythmic humming or strumming sound, a word used for describing a beat.

clue.text: OSCAR?

parts.note: read as OS CAR: OS is outsize, so an outsize motor

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals let OSCAR split into OS, the clothing abbreviation for outsize, and CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A limo, short for limousine, is a very large luxurious car.

clue.text: 14 (2000) featuring boy, single victim of swamp attack?

indicators.note: a victim of an alligator ends up inside it, so these letters are swallowed

parts.note: an alligator, or gator, is the attacker of the swamp
a lad is a boy
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A film is said to star a boy, the lone casualty of an alligator in the marshes.
explanation.walkthrough: The swamp's attacker is an alligator; its victim ends up inside it, so 'victim of' swallows the boy and the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ridley Scott's Gladiator won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 2000.

clue.text: Rank request

definitions.meaning: a class or grade, as in a social stratum
a command or a purchase asked for, as in a restaurant

explanation.definitionFit: Order means both a level in a hierarchy and a demand or request for goods.

clue.text: Founder of the Academy broadcasting 14 (1986)

parts.note: the Greek philosopher Plato founded the Academy in Athens
a programme being broadcast is on air

explanation.surface: An ancient philosopher is on air introducing a 1986 film.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Stone's Vietnam War film Platoon won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 1986.

clue.text: 14 (2004) featuring Billy Idol (abnormal cast)

indicators.note: to cast is to shape or throw, so these letters are reformed into a new order

parts.note: the rock singer's name, taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A film supposedly stars rock singer Billy Idol in an unusual line-up of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like the film's actors but is the anagram signal; 'abnormal' is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Clint Eastwood's boxing drama won the Academy Award for Best Picture for 2004.
